name: Grace Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive an underground haul truck at the Holloway zinc mine. It's a low, long truck that carries ore up the ramp from the bottom of the mine to the surface, about forty minutes each way, in the dark with just your lights. I'm on day and night swing, a week of each. I like the rhythm and the trust you build with the other drivers on the radio, and I don't like it when the ramp's wet and you're crawling up with twenty-five tonnes behind you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner, Callum, in a rented house in Stanmoor. He's a second-year apprentice plumber, so we're both on small wages and we've got about three weeks of money in the bank. My mum and dad have a small sheep farm twenty minutes out, and I'm there most days off helping with the shearing or the fences. I'm also in the volunteer fire brigade, which is the best thing in this town, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't mind that at all. Our grandparents managed without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's get on with real work. I'd probably say it at the fire station on training night, because that's where the gossip happens. I'm not much for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Callum finishes his apprenticeship, I keep driving, and we might save a house deposit in a few years. That's what I want, a normal life near my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep helping on the farm, and start putting a set amount away each pay, maybe eighty a fortnight. I'd use the AI app now and then to sort Mum's farm accounts, like I did last tax time. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Mum's farm accounts. How did that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than I expected. It sorted the receipts into the right boxes, and I checked it twice. Mum still doesn't believe a computer did it, she thinks I'm secretly good at maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a normal life near family look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own house with a bit of land, close enough to help Mum and Dad when they get older. Sunday roast at the farm. Kids one day, but not yet, not on these wages.

S0.say: She'd say good, now let's get on with real work, most likely at the fire station on training night rather than online.
S0.think: She sees this picture as letting her partner finish his apprenticeship and her keep driving, so they might save a house deposit and live near her family.
S0.do: Keeps working and helping on her parents' farm, and starts saving about eighty a fortnight. Uses an AI app now and then for her mother's farm accounts.
S0.quote: Mum still doesn't believe a computer did it, she thinks I'm secretly good at maths.
S0.fieldNote: Grace's goals are traditional and local: a house near her parents' farm and a family later. She already uses AI for small practical tasks but checks its work. Community life through the fire brigade matters a lot to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can picture. They've talked about driverless trucks underground at the big mines overseas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and you can't stop progress, but the company should give local people first go at the new jobs. Train the people who already know the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think driving is exactly the kind of job that shrinks. I'm average, I'm not the best driver on the ramp. If they cut half the drivers, I'd be fifty-fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch how the first group gets on with the new control system, then put my hand up for it within the year. I'd keep saving and help out more on the farm for extra money. And I'd keep an eye on jobs at the processing plant above ground, where they'd still need people for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like a cough that won't go away, not serious yet but you notice it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if you lost the job in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Companies have to compete, that's how it works. I'd be cross if they didn't train locals, though, that's where I'd draw the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Callum's job be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, I don't think. Robots aren't crawling under houses fixing pipes in this picture. Which is funny, because he was the one I was worried about when he started.

S1.say: She'd say it's progress that can't be stopped, but the company should give local people first go at new jobs and train those who know the mine.
S1.think: She thinks driving is exactly the kind of job that shrinks and, as an average driver, gives herself even odds of keeping her place.
S1.do: Watches how the first group handles the new control system, then applies within the year. Keeps saving, earns a bit more on the farm and watches for jobs at the processing plant.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cough that won't go away.
S1.quote: It's like a cough that won't go away, not serious yet but you notice it.
S1.fieldNote: Grace accepts automation as progress and doesn't blame the company, but insists on local hiring. She's frank that her skill is average. She notes the irony that her partner's trade now looks safer than her job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and towns need to pull together, because nobody's going to save us from outside. I'd say it at the brigade and at the pub. I'd probably say the government should stay out of the way and let people build new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. If robots can do the plumbing too, then Callum's apprenticeship might be finished before he is. We'd both be out with three weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd give up the rental and move onto the farm, into the old cottage Dad keeps saying he'll fix. I'd work every shift I could at the mine until it ended. I'd cut everything, and I'd help Dad try to make the farm earn more, maybe selling meat direct to people in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake listening to Callum sleep and doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should stay out of the way. Would you take government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came, I'd take it for a while, I'm not stupid. But I'd rather have a job than a payment. I'd feel better earning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get onto the farm and get the cottage livable. That's about it. You can't build a new life in two years, you can just move into the one you've got.

S2.say: She'd say families and towns must pull together because nobody will save them from outside, and that government should stay out of the way and let people build new things.
S2.think: She's scared that robots could take her partner's plumbing trade too, leaving them both out of work with three weeks of savings.
S2.do: Gives up the rental to live in the old cottage on her parents' farm and works every mine shift until it ends. Cuts all spending and helps her father make the farm earn more, perhaps by selling meat directly.
S2.quote: You can't build a new life in two years, you can just move into the one you've got.
S2.fieldNote: Grace's safety net is family land, not government, and she'd move onto the farm at once. She'd take public help reluctantly but would rather earn. The threat to her partner's trade turns this from one job at risk to two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better. That's enough for Callum to finish his ticket at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's be practical and use the time, and that locals should get first pick of whatever new work the mine has. I'd say it at the brigade and probably at a council meeting if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years gives us one move. I'd want to get onto the surface side or the control room, and save as much as possible. After 2031, I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the control room training once the first group had done it, probably in year two. We'd put off the house deposit and keep renting, and build up savings instead, aiming for three months. I'd keep helping on the farm, because that's our safety net either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was doing something. That's better than lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off the house deposit, how would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. We've had the spot picked out for a while, on Ridge Lane near the farm. But I'd rather rent with savings than own with nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You wait for the first group again. In five years, isn't waiting a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've seen people rush into things at Holloway and get burnt. A year of watching is worth it, as long as I don't sit on my hands after that.

S3.say: She'd say people should be practical and use the time, with locals getting first pick of new mine work, raising it at the brigade and council meetings.
S3.think: She thinks five years gives them one move: into the surface or control room side while saving hard. Beyond 2031 she doesn't know.
S3.do: Signs up for control room training in about year two after the first group has done it. Postpones the house deposit to build three months of savings and keeps helping on the farm as a safety net.
S3.feel: Anxious but active, which beats lying awake.
S3.quote: But I'd rather rent with savings than own with nothing in the bank.
S3.fieldNote: Grace stays a careful second mover even with a deadline, because she's seen rushed changes go wrong. She'd sacrifice the house plan for savings. The family farm is her backup in every scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long time, but it goes fast, Mum always says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been told early, so people should get on with it. Train up, save up, and look after your own. Nobody should be surprised in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be all right for most of it. Callum would be a qualified plumber, I'd be on the control side or the farm. The worry is right at the end, with robots on farms and in houses too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep driving and we'd still save for the house, but slower. I'd do the control room training once it'd proven itself, and maybe a farm business course at night, because one day the farm might come to me. We'd plan on kids around year five, if work held.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly hopeful, but uneasy about the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to run the farm one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once I'd seen it work on a farm like ours. Not some big operation, a small one. If it saves Dad's back, I'd be all for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, we're moving into the old cottage with nothing. With ten, we might be living in it because we chose to, with a plan. Same cottage, different story.

S4.say: She'd say people have been warned early, so they should train, save and look after their own; nobody should be surprised in 2036.
S4.think: She thinks they'd be fine for most of the decade, with her partner qualified and her on the control side or the farm; the worry is the very end, when robots reach farms and homes.
S4.do: Keeps driving and saves more slowly for a house in year one. Does control room training once proven and a night-time farm business course, and plans to have children around year five if work holds.
S4.quote: With two, we're moving into the old cottage with nothing. With ten, we might be living in it because we chose to, with a plan. Same cottage, different story.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Grace fold the change into her long-term family plan, including taking over the farm. She'd use AI on the farm once proven on a small operation like theirs. Her answers stay rooted in family and place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it'd hit me and Callum at once, before he's even qualified. What would help is the mine training local people first, and help for small family farms so we've got somewhere to fall back on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the brigade. If the mine goes, half our volunteers go with it, and then who turns up when there's a fire on the hill? That's the bit people in cities don't see.

headlineQuote: If the mine goes, half our volunteers go with it, and then who turns up when there's a fire on the hill?
portrait: Grace Jensen is a 27-year-old underground haul truck driver at the Holloway zinc mine, renting in Stanmoor with her partner Callum, an apprentice plumber, with about three weeks of savings. She's traditional and community-minded, spends her days off on her parents' sheep farm and volunteers with the fire brigade. She uses AI now and then and adopts new things once others have tested them. A plateau leaves her content and steady change uneasy, while AGI in two years alarms her and sends them to live on the farm. With five and ten years, she plans control room training, delays the house and builds towards taking on the farm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit her and her partner at the same time, before he's even qualified.
whatWouldHelp: The mine training local people first, and help for small family farms so families have somewhere to fall back on.
